Good morning. The 108th plenary meeting of the General Assembly is called to order. Before proceeding further, it is my sad duty to pay tribute to the memory of His Majesty King Harald V of Norway, who passed away on August 28, 2026. On behalf of the Assembly, I convey our condolences to the government and people of Norway, to the bereaved family of His Majesty King Harald V. I now invite representatives to stand and observe a minute of silence in tribute to the memory of His Majesty King Harald V. I thank you. I would also like to extend my condolences to the families of the victims of the severe flooding in Nepal and China, which has claimed many lives, left people missing, and caused widespread destruction. The Assembly will begin its high-level meeting to commemorate and promote the International Day against Nuclear Tests in accordance with resolution 72/51 of December 4, 2017, and resume its consideration of agenda item 99 entitled General and Complete Disarmament. I will now make a statement as the President of the General Assembly. Executive Secretary of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization, Dr. Robert Floyd, Under Secretary General Nagamitsu, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. Frankly speaking, if you had asked me a few years ago why we commemorate international days such as this, I might have thought it is a bit outdated. Yet we are not living in 2015, but in 2026, a time of increased geopolitical tension, more armed conflict than ever, and unfortunately, declining trust between member states when the risk of miscalculation and escalation demand sustained attention. We also live in an era of rapid technological change, where the potential application of artificial intelligence to nuclear weapons systems raises serious questions about decision making, human control, and the risk of miscalculation. Of course, Some may ask also why should we be so concerned about testing when more often than not it happens far away in the middle of an ocean or desert. But history has shown us that the first step towards something far more serious and far more sinister is indeed testing. One need only look at the first nuclear test on July 16, 1945 in New Mexico. that test ushered in a new era in which warfare for the first time carried the possibility of destruction on an existential scale. Reality demonstrated with brutal clarity just weeks later in Hiroshima and Nagasaki. And in an interconnected world such as ours, there is no truly remote region. immune from the effects or dangers of nuclear testing. Across the world, from Lop Nur in China and the atolls of the Pacific to Nevada, Algeria, Western Australia, and the South Atlantic, atmospheric nuclear tests released an estimated explosive yield of approximately 438 megatons. equivalent to more than 29,000 Hiroshima-sized nuclear bombs. The human and environmental consequences have been immense. At Semipalatinsk alone, between 1949 and 1962, hundreds of thousands of people living nearby were exposed to elevated levels of radiation. For many survivors, these are not distant chapters of history, but lived experiences carried within families and across generations. The effects do not end with the immediate explosion, but linger in contained land and water, in agriculture, livestock, and food change, and in the people's life and communities, particularly indigenous communities. exposed to radiation. We all know that commemorating an international day or even remembering history does not necessarily mean we are wiser or better able to avert threats. Yet, Days such this remain important opportunities to reflect on, especially at a time when we are witnessing not only, as said in the beginning, rising conflict and geopolitical tensions, but growing pressure on this institution and on the multilateral agreements it has helped to forge. The Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty is a case in point. 30 years after it opened for signature, the treaty is still not entered into force because the remaining required ratifications have not been secured. For some, that is evidence of the limitation of multilateralism. But days like today give us an opportunity to push back against that narrative. to ensure that we do not allow the story of this institution or of this treaty to be rewritten solely in terms of what I said not achieved yet. Because the treaty also tells a remarkable story of what multilateralism has indeed achieved. Before the treaty opened for signature, more than 2,000 nuclear test explosions had been conducted worldwide. Since 1996, that number has fallen to fewer than a dozen. That is the true measure of its impact of this special treaty. And it is a success we must build on by providing the international monitoring system with the political and financial support needed to ensure reliable and timely data, by strengthening the CTBTO and the IAEA alongside bilateral and multilateral agreements, and by renewing the political and financial commitments we made in the Pact for the Future. Because even without its entry into force, the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty has proven its worth time and again. Its success can be measured not only by what has happened over the past 30 years, but by what has not happened. 81 years ago, Hiroshima was the first nuclear disaster. In building this house of diplomacy, our forefathers and mothers promised that Nagasaki would be the last. And for more than 80 years, it has been. So it is upon us to build on this eight-decade-long success for multilateralism. to ensure that it lasts for another 80 years. I thank you. In accordance with rule 70 of the rules of procedure of the Assembly, I now give the floor to Ms. Izumi Nakamitsu, Under-Secretary-General and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs, who will deliver a statement on behalf of the Secretary-General, His Excellency Antonio Guterres.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, at the outset, allow me to thank the President of the General Assembly, Her Excellency Ms. Annalena Baerbock, for convening this important annual commemoration. Madam President, thank you so much. I also thank Kazakhstan for its enduring leadership in establishing this day and ensuring that the legacy of nuclear testing is never forgotten. As we mark 35 years since the closure of the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site, that historic decision reminds us that remembrance must go hand in hand with responsibility. I extend particular thanks to today's keynote speakers who bring to this hall the voices of communities affected by the horrors of nuclear testing and the scientific experts dedicated to ensuring it never happens again. Their testimonies and expertise will ground our deliberations in both lived experience and evidence. I want to take this opportunity to commend Dr. Robert Floyd, Executive Secretary of the Preparatory Commission for the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization, and the Provisional Technical Secretariat for their continued efforts to advance the CTBT's universalization and strengthen its verification regime. Excellencies, we must remember why this day exists. The Secretary-General's message is clear. The world must never witness another nuclear explosion. Not even one, whatever its stated purpose or intent. That is the promise embodied in this day and the responsibility entrusted to us. Yet we meet amid deep geopolitical tension, growing division, and diminishing trust. Against this backdrop, concerns about the possible resumption of nuclear explosive testing have reemerged in recent years. Even contemplating such a course is dangerous. Any resumption would erode decades of restraints, deepen mistrust, and risk triggering reciprocal tests and an arms race. This must never become reality. This year marks the 30th anniversary of the CTBT's opening for signature. Since then, the treaty has helped establish a powerful global norm against nuclear testing. Its verification regime stands as a remarkable achievement in multilateral disarmament and non-proliferation. Together, the International Monitoring System and the International Data Centre provide objective and reliable data to help detect and locate events and assess whether they may indicate a nuclear explosion. Yet, one central challenge remains. The CTBT is not in force. Its technical achievements are significant, but only the treaty's entry into force can establish a permanent, legally binding prohibition on nuclear testing and unlock the CTBT's full potential. The treaty already enjoys near-universal support. Tonga's ratification last month brought the number of ratifying states to 179. The remaining Annex II states must sign and/or ratify the CTBT without further delay and without conditions. Until then, all states possessing nuclear weapons must maintain moratoria on all nuclear explosive testing. There can be no exceptions and no return to the past. Distinguished delegates, the urgency of these steps is measured not only in strategic risk, but also in human suffering and environmental damage. Nuclear tests have scarred lives, lands, and descendants. Their consequences have crossed borders and generations. Communities continue to live with harm that was not of their making. The natural environment continues to bear damage that no political declaration can simply undo. As the Secretary-General reminds us, their suffering is not history, it's a warning. The voices of those affected by nuclear testing are not echoes from a distant past. They must guide the choices we make in the present. We owe them more than remembrance. Our attention, our support, and decisive action to ensure that such harm is never again inflicted on any person, community, or environment. Excellencies, nearly 30 years after the CDBT opened for signature, The world possesses the knowledge and tools to end nuclear testing for good. All that remains is the political will to act. Let this day renew our common commitment. Not one more nuclear explosion and no further delay in bringing the CTBT into force. We owe this to the victims and survivors. We owe it to their descendants. And we owe it to every generation that follows. I thank you very much for your attention.

I thank the Under-Secretary-General and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs. Before proceeding further and as indicated in my letter dated August 24th, 2026, I should like to consult members with a view to inviting the following speakers to deliver opening and keynote addresses at this commemorative meeting. Mr. Robert Floyd, Executive Secretary of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization, Ms. Tina Cordova, co-founder of the Tula Rosa Basin Downwinders Consortium, Miss Magdalene Wangui Wanyaga, geoscientist, expert on the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization Verification Regime and member of the organization's scientific program committee, and Mr. Karibek Kuyukov, artist, humanitarian advocate and a goodwill ambassador of Kazakhstan. May I take it that it is the wish of the Assembly, without setting a precedent, to invite these speakers to make statements at this commemorative meeting? It is so decided. I therefore give the floor to Mr. Robert Floyd, Executive Secretary of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization. Please, the floor is yours.

President, Under-Secretary-General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I'm honored to address the General Assembly on this important occasion. In 2009, this Assembly responded to an excellent initiative from Kazakhstan. It proclaimed the 29th of August as the International Day Against Nuclear Tests. Why this day? Because on the 29th of August 1991, the Semipalatinsk nuclear weapon testing site in today's Kazakhstan was shut down. Between 1949 and 1989, that one site saw 456 nuclear tests. 456 tests at that one site. But this was not the only site. Those were not the only tests. Since 1945, our planet has seen more than 2,000 nuclear test explosions. The vast majority of those tests took place before 1996. But in the past three decades, fewer than 12 nuclear weapon explosive tests have been detected and announced. The Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty has helped create a new global norm, a norm against any nuclear testing. Friends, today we are close to universality. Almost every state on earth has joined the CTBT. Only last month the Kingdom of Tonga joined the CTBT family and our congratulations to Tonga on both signing and ratifying. 188 states have now signed, 179 have ratified. Every country that has signed the treaty and most of the eight that have not, they actually support the object and purpose of the treaty. We've come so far. From those long decades of nuclear testing seeming normal to today's international norm against nuclear testing. So how has the CTBT made this happen? We've set up the International Monitoring System, the IMS, a technological marvel. It's now over 90% complete. 308 certified networked facilities working day and night to the highest agreed international scientific standards, checking for nuclear tests in the oceans, on every continent, in the atmosphere. Every day, we take in some 36 gigabytes of data. And all that data is available to every CTBT state signatory, transparently, equally, fairly. Technology and analysis techniques have galloped forward since the treaty was opened for signature in 1996. Our systems today can detect tests far smaller than what the treaty negotiators expected. The IMS was originally designed to detect tests that were a yield of 1,000 tons of TNT equivalent. But today, the IMS detection goes down to 500 tons. That is just over 3% of the power of the bomb that devastated Hiroshima. Amazingly sensitive. But 500 tonnes is not zero tonnes. The treaty bans all nuclear tests, however big, however tiny. And any nuclear test is a matter of grave concern. The CTBT success is built on science, but it's also built on confidence. Today, the science is working, but the confidence is under strain. We must be clear-eyed about the need to build confidence, especially for low-yield testing below the level of 500 tonnes. There are steps that can be taken today, even now. And ultimately, we must keep striving for the best solution that tomorrow promises, entry into force of the CTBT. Friends, 2026 is our Treaty's 30th anniversary year. We celebrate something extraordinary. The CTBT has worked as intended. A near halt to nuclear testing since 1996. A remarkable success. But have we guaranteed a verifiable end to all nuclear testing once and for all? No one here today needs reminding. The international scene is tense, full of mistrust. Those tensions extend to discussions around returning to nuclear testing. Imagine our world if the CTBT falters and the norm against nuclear testing collapses. A world with unconstrained testing using all of today's technology. A world where suspected tests are not even worth debating because it has become normal again. Old nuclear arsenals expand, new nuclear arsenals are built, nuclear proliferation runs rampant. Soaring risk of nuclear miscalculation. Risks of nuclear misadventure. Devastation from nuclear bad luck. Friends, this is not the world that we have. And this is not the world that we've worked so hard to build. And this is not the world that we strive for. So let us make sure it is not the world that we leave behind. Thank you.
I thank the Executive Secretary for the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization. I now give the floor to Ms. Tina Cordova, co-founder of the Tularosa Basin Downwinders Consortium.

Madam President, esteemed members of the Assembly, good morning. And thank you for inviting me to deliver these remarks today. My name is Tina Cordova and I'm from Tularosa, New Mexico. I'm a business owner who started a business 36 years ago with my partner Russ Steward. But I am not here because of that. I am here because I am a mother, a grandmother, and a soon to be great grandmother. And I co-founded an organization 21 years ago called the Tularosa Basin Downwinders Consortium. Our mission has been to bring attention to the negative health effects suffered by the people of New Mexico as a result of being overexposed to radiation from the development and testing of the atomic bomb detonated at the Trinity site. We were the first people exposed to radiation any place in the world as ash fell from the sky in the days after the bomb. We were never warned before or after of the danger, so we lived our lives off the land as we always did. We're referred to as downwinders, and while we were the first, we are certainly not the only downwinders. The nuclear testing that took place all across the world has likely produced millions of downwinders, people that lived in places like Guam, Idaho, Utah, Arizona, Nevada, Colorado, and Montana, but also people from the French Polynesian island of Tahiti and Kazakhstan and the Aboriginal people from Australia. And we have the uranium miners and workers and their families who live adjacent to abandoned uranium mine and mill sites in places like Laguna and Acoma Pueblo and across the Navajo Nation. All people who've been horribly harmed just like us. We're the people that became the collateral damage to the development and testing of nuclear devices, and we were left to deal with the consequences on our own. We carry the genetic footprint in our bodies and pass it on. In doing this work, I don't know of anyone who died the day of Trinity. However, it was the beginning of the end for tens of thousands of people that we've documented, including babies that died in record numbers in the year after Trinity. Babies died and no one has ever returned to assess the situation, much less atone for it. I'm here to speak up for the many people whose voices were silenced, who cry out from their graves, the babies and the children whose voices were silenced or whose voices were never heard. People like those in my own family. I had two great grandfathers alive at the time of the bomb living in Tularosa, 45 miles away the crows fly from the test site, 45 miles. In 1955, they were both told they had stomach cancer. They were given morphine and sent home. They suffered and died. They were the first generation. I had two grandmothers alive at the time of Trinity. They both developed cancer. They were the second generation. My father, Anastacio Cordova, was a four-year-old child living a very organic lifestyle the day of the bomb. He, like everyone else, dipped rainwater from the cistern, ate an abundance of fresh produce and meat, hunted, and drank mass quantities of fresh cow's milk. In his late 50s, he got cancer at the base of his tongue. He had to have part of his tongue removed along with all the lymph nodes in his neck. He had massive quantities of radiation and lost all his beautiful, perfect white teeth. He lived on a feeding tube for over 18 months, losing over 60 pounds. He survived only to get prostate cancer, which was so much easier on him. And eight years after the first lesion, he developed an all new cancer on the forward part of his tongue. It was not metastatic. And when I asked the oncologist, how does this happen to a man who doesn't smoke, rarely drinks alcohol, has no viruses, and would never put chewing tobacco in his mouth? I was told it doesn't happen, but we see it all the time in New Mexico. My dad suffered in ways I could never adequately describe, and then he died. He was the third generation. I was diagnosed with thyroid cancer at the age of 39, and the first question they asked me was, when were you exposed to radiation? I knew that my exposure came from living so close to a test site. I was the fourth generation. My mother, Rosalie, is being followed for a tumor that so far is benign. I have one sister. She's had skin cancer. I have two brothers. My youngest brother was diagnosed with kidney cancer 18 months ago at the age of 52. If that weren't bad enough, his only daughter was diagnosed with thyroid cancer at the age of 23, and she's had so many complications. She's the fifth generation. My family is not unique in New Mexico or in any of the places where people have been exposed to radiation from nuclear testing. We've documented thousands of families like mine exhibiting four and five generations of cancer in places like Carrizozo, Socorro, Mescalero, La Luz, and Alamogordo, all the forgotten cities of Trinity where people have been dying for generations. Many people stand side by side with me in this fight. I don't do this work alone, and our organization of volunteers has structure and meaning and strategy, and we commit ourselves every day to do this work because we have families, children and grandchildren that we love and cherish. I know that each of us present here today has a heart that beats the same and a soul that longs for peace and well-being. I know we have the ability to work together as human beings with a shared vision to eliminate nuclear testing and the use of nuclear weapons so we never create another victim. We owe our children and our grandchildren so much more than what happened in the past. I recall these words spoken by President John F. Kennedy when he addressed the American public in July 1963 during the nuclear test ban treaty negotiations, he said, The loss of even one human life or the malformation of one baby who may be born long after all of us have gone should be of concern to us all. Our children and grandchildren are not merely statistics towards which we can be indifferent. I agree with President Kennedy, but it took 60 years after that speech for the people of New Mexico to be acknowledged for their sacrifice and their suffering. Those of us gathered here today cannot be held accountable for the sins of the past, but I know for certain we most assuredly should be held accountable if we repeat them. After 81 years, it's time we set our families, our children, and our grandchildren free from nuclear threat. We must commit ourselves to a world without nuclear testing, a world without nuclear weapons. Thank you.

I thank Mrs. Cordova for sharing the tremendous effects to your family. I give the floor to Ms. Magdalene Bangui Bangyaga, geoscientist, expert on the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization Verification Regime, and member of the organization's scientific program committee.

Thank you. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues and friends, it's an honor to address this assembly on this day of the International Day Against Nuclear Testing. My name is Magdalene Wongoi Wanyaga, and I'm a geoscientist from Kenya with a background in applied geophysics and seismology. My journey has taken me from analyzing seismic data at the Kenya National Data Center to contributing to the work of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization, including as a youth group education coordinator in the past and briefing the United Nations Security Council, as well as today serving as a working group B task leader. I share this because my experience has taught me that science is not separate from peace and security. It can be one of the foundations. Today is particularly significant as we mark the International Day Against Nuclear Weapon Testing in the same year as we commemorate 30 years since the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty was opened for signature. This day reminds us of the devastating effects of nuclear testing and the need for its cessation as part of our pursuit of a nuclear weapon-free world. The CTBT bans all nuclear test explosions, whether for military or civilian purposes. This establishing a global norm supported by a verification regime that provides the scientific means to monitor compliance. The scale of what has been achieved is remarkable. In the five decades before the treaty was opened for signature in 1996, more than 2,000 nuclear weapon tests were conducted around the world. And since then, fewer than a dozen have been conducted. That near silent is not an accident. It's an achievement. At the heart of this achievement is the international monitoring system through seismic, hydroacoustic, infrasound, and radionuclide technologies. 300 monitoring facilities around the world provide the capability to detect nuclear explosions and strengthen confidence in compliance. This is what makes the norm credible. And the value of this science extends beyond nuclear security. The CTBTO data supports tsunami warnings, tracking of radioactive releases during nuclear emergencies. aviation safety around volcanic eruptions, and research on the Earth, climate, oceans, and atmosphere. Scientists around the world can also use this selected data to advance research and generate new knowledge. These are civilian and scientific benefits from a system created for international peace and security. Personally, this is personal. My early work as a seismic analyst introduced me to this scientific community, and showed me how technical expertise can cross borders and serve a purpose greater than any one institution or country. This experience also inspired me to initiate Sensors Terra, an effort to strengthen seismic monitoring in Kenya and in Africa. This brings me to the people behind the science. This year also marks 10 years of the CBT youth group and I am proud to have been part of that journey. Over the past decade, the youth group has demonstrated that young people are simply not the future of the CBT, we are part of its presence. We, young scientists bring new ideas and technologies. Young professions bring different disciplines and perspectives. Young people from different regions bring experiences that can challenge assumptions and broaden how we understand security. My experience with the youth group has reinforced the meaning of participation is not just about representation alone. It's also about creating opportunities to contribute, and this must extend beyond the youth. Women, early career scientists and experts from developing countries should have meaningful opportunities to contribute to scientific programs, policy discussions and the global decision making. Democratizing STEM and global governance means creating meaningful opportunities for diverse voices to contribute regardless of the geography, age, gender, discipline or access. Excellencies, 30 years after the CTBT opened for signature, we have seen what a strong international norm supported by science and multilateral cooperation can achieve. But the work is not finished. The treaty has yet to enter into force. We must contribute to strengthen the norm against nuclear testing, sustain the scientific capacity that verifies it, and invest in people who carry this work forward. On this International Day Against Nuclear Testing, let us remember not only what the international community has achieved, but what we still have an opportunity to achieve. A world without nuclear testing is possible. The CTBT provides the pathway. Science provides confidence and the next generation must carry it forward. Thank you.
I thank Miss Vanyaga. I now give the floor to Mr. Karibek Kuyukov, artist, humanitarian advocate and the Goodwill Ambassador of Kazakhstan.

Ladies

and gentlemen, first and foremost, I would like to thank the organizers of today's conference. Thank you for the opportunity to speak on behalf of Kazakhstan. On the 29th of August, and Kazakhstan and all over the world, we commemorate the International Day Against Nuclear Tests. This day is the same day when the Semipalatinsk test site was closed down, a site where for 40 years nuclear tests were conducted. My people managed to put an end to this in 1989. For the first time, In the history of the 20th century, the people of an entire nation rose up in defense of their lives. Back in the 1990s, we didn't have the internet, we didn't have cell phones, so we sent a letter to Moscow, and it worked. On the 20th of November, 1989, the USSR leadership adopted a decision tasking the government to shut down the Semipalatinsk test site. Swiftly, we managed to include this item in the declaration of independence of the Kazakh SSR. On the territory of Kazakhstan, nuclear test ban is in force. No test sites for other types of weapons WMDs that is, are allowed to be built. This applies also to chemical weapons, bacteriological weapons and biological weapons. The construction of such test sites is prohibited. In January of 1991, we were closer than ever to a global ban on nuclear weapons. The International Anti-Nuclear Alliance held a meeting at UN headquarters. We pooled all of the anti-war, anti-nuclear forces from all corners of the world. Back then, Kazakhstan achieved a special status. Ever since then, we've been known as the leaders of the anti-nuclear movement the world over. Throughout the history of tests being conducted in Semipalatinsk, the government stated that one and a half million people were victims of that testing, although the real number is much higher, of course. My parents witnessed this. My mother, before I was born, well, she had two children. One of those children died before he turned one. After that, the second child died as well. After those two infant deaths, I was born without any arms. The delivery was very difficult for my mother. And there were many such victims. Now, I'm a creative person, and I couldn't remain silent. In my paintings, I try to draw attention to this problem. Once, I went to a medical facility in the city of Semipalatinsk. There, there is a museum in honor of the victims of radiation. On the shelves, you have glass beakers, and you have all sorts of terrible fetuses in ethanol. And this made me understand that my fate could have been the same as that of those fetuses. That's when I took the decision to honor the memory of everyone who suffered to fight nuclear weapons for as long as I have the force to do so. Currently, The situation on our planet is very tense. People are threatening to wage war on one another. And what's most important, the innocent victims of such wars are children. It is high time to radically change the situation. And the only way to do this is together, joining hands. We cannot look idly by, indifferent. We cannot afford to wait. We must forgive past errors. Yes, this is our history, but history is in the rear view mirror. It's in the past. Therefore, to build a new world, we need to come to grips with, once again, with what is good, what is compassion. We are duty bound to bequeath a safe world for our children. For 35 years, Kazakhstan has lived without any nuclear tests. Over 100 different religious and ethnic groups live in Kazakhstan. I believe that this is an excellent example for other countries to look up to. Does humanity need nuclear weapons? Unfortunately, this question remains relevant. We must work together to answer it, to find a solution. Thank you for your kind attention. I wish peace and prosperity for all of your families. Thank you.

Thank you. I thank Mr. Kuyukov for sharing your personal story. before proceeding further as agreed at the general committee meeting on May 18th 2026 and announced in the president's letter dated May 20th 2026 I propose that the time limits for statements in this commemorative meeting be 3 minutes for delegation speaking in their national capacity and 5 minutes for statements on behalf of a group of states is there any objection to this proposal I hear none it is so decided Accordingly, pursuant to Rule 72 of the Rules of Procedure of the Assembly, when a representative exceeds her or his allotted time, the President shall call the speaker to order without delay, which will be done by means of automatic microphone cut-off. As the first speaker, I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Burundi, who will speak on behalf of the African States.

Madam President,

it is an honor for me to deliver this statement on behalf of the Africa Group. The Africa Group would like to extend its gratitude to the President of the General Assembly. Thank you for convening this meeting. We also wish to thank the UN Secretary-General for his message and his very valuable support to the endeavour of nuclear disarmament. This year marks the 81st anniversary of the first nuclear weapons test and the nuclear bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. This is a searing reminder of the existential threat posed by nuclear weapons to humanity, to humanity but also to international peace and security. Over 2000 nuclear tests have been conducted all over the world. Our group remains deeply disquieted by the humanitarian and environmental consequences thereof, which are devastating. Today, we're meeting in this chamber and we must reiterate our collective determination to raise awareness amongst the general public so as to prevent any resumption of explosive nuclear tests with a view to advancing the cause of the total elimination of nuclear weapons. Putting an end to nuclear tests is an important step on the way towards a world free from nuclear weapons. The commemorations we are involved in this year is therefore particularly important because it also marks the 30th anniversary of the opening for signature of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, the CTBT. The African continent knows firsthand the lasting ramifications of nuclear tests. Now, this experience has shaped our early and unswerving commitment, the commitment of Africa to nuclear disarmament, which paved the way for the Pelindaba Treaty, which established Africa as a nuclear weapons free zone, banning testing of nuclear explosive devices across our entire continent. The Africa Group would like to express its full support for maintaining the existing moratorium on nuclear tests conducted by nuclear weapons states until the CTBT enters into force. We call on nuclear weapons states to abstain from engaging in any activities or in rhetoric which suggest that nuclear tests of any kind might be resumed. which is at odds with the principles and purposes of the CTBT. Madam President, the total elimination of nuclear weapons is the only way of ensuring an absolute guarantee that they will not be used, nor will there be a threat of them being used. Thus, the group reaffirms that the devastating humanitarian consequences and the risks intrinsic to nuclear weapons beef up the legal, ethical, and security imperatives of achieving nuclear disarmament. They also speak to the urgency of achieving a nuclear weapons-free world that must be upheld. The African Group would like to underscore the need of placing humanitarian considerations at the heart of all discussions on nuclear weapons. We remain particularly concerned about the devastating consequences of any nuclear weapons detonation, whether that be the result of an accident, a miscalculation, or a deliberate act. Therefore, we call on all States in particular the nuclear weapons states, to fully factor in the catastrophic and lasting consequences of the use of nuclear weapons and the testing thereof, consequences for human health, the environment and sustainable development. We urge them to take concrete and irreversible measures so as to ensure the total elimination of their nuclear arsenals. The group supports the principle of complete nuclear disarmament. This is a necessary prerequisite for the maintenance of international peace and security. It is in this spirit that we would like to recall the NPT, as well as the historic entry into force of the Total Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons Treaty, the objective being to complete, to add to the NPT and to advance nuclear disarmament banning it in a comprehensive fashion, banning the testing of nuclear weapons. Thus, the group would like to urge all nuclear weapons states and states -- the speaker's microphone has been cut off.

The distinguished -- I thank the distinguished representative of Burundi. Thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Andorra, who will speak on behalf of the members of the group of Western European and other states, followed by Australia and Uruguay.

Madam President, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the members of the Western European and other states group. Nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation remain indispensable to upholding international peace and security. As we commemorate International Day Against Nuclear Test this year, the prohibition of all nuclear weapon test explosion continues as an essential objective in our collective efforts towards a safer and more peaceful world. 35 years ago, the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site in Kazakhstan was closed. marking an important milestone in the global effort to put an end to nuclear weapon testing. This milestone was the core of the adoption of the General Assembly Resolution 64/35 in 2009, which declared 29 August International Day Against Nuclear Test, drawing attention to the need to enhance public awareness and education about the effects of nuclear weapon test explosion or any other nuclear explosion. Resolution 64/35 also reaffirms the importance of ending all nuclear tests in the pursuit of a nuclear-weapon-free world. Madam President, this year we commemorate 30 years since the opening for the signature of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. The Treaty, with its universal support, near universal support, remains fundamental to achieving and sustaining nuclear disarmament, as it has helped to sustain the global norm against nuclear testing. In this regard, we welcome the universalization of the Treaty in the Pacific following the recent signature and ratification by the Kingdom of Tonga. We commend the continued efforts of the Executive Secretary of the Preparatory Commission, Mr Robert Floyd, to advance ratifications. Moreover, we call on States to do more to advance the universalization of the Treaty to ensure its entry into force. This should include efforts at the upcoming 12th Ministerial Meeting of the Friends of the CTBT on 22 September, as well as the high-level meeting to mark International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons on 29 September. That will take place on the margins of the General Debate of the 81st... General Assembly and by supporting the annual CTBT resolutions at the First Committee. Madam President, the members of the WIOP strongly and unequivocally condemn Russia's illegal and unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine, which is a flagrant violation of international law, including Article 2.4 of the UN Charter, and undermines the principle of territorial integrity. Russia's evocation of its ratification of CTBT seriously undermines its about commitment to ongoing non-proliferation and disarmament efforts. The members of the group also condemn in the strongest terms the sixth nuclear test conducted by the Democratic People's Republic of Korea since 2006 in violation of relevant Security Council resolutions. We call for full compliance with the UN Security Council resolutions, including the complete, verifiable and irreversible abandonment of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea's nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs, and an end to the further nuclear test. We also support the peaceful denuclearization of the Korean peninsula and call the DPRK to resume dialogue. Madam President, ladies and gentlemen, in conclusion, the members of the group reaffirm its commitment to final and irreversible cessation of all nuclear test explosions. We call on governments, international, regional and sub-regional organizations, as well as civil society, academia and individuals to work with us and advance the common cause of a world free of nuclear weapons. Thank you for listening.

I thank the distinguished representative of Andorra. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Australia. Just before that, I would like to inform the Assembly that the President has received requests from additional Member States to speak in this commemorative meeting. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Australia on behalf of the Group of Friends of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty.

Thank you, President. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the friends of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, comprising Australia, Canada, Finland, Germany, Japan, and the Netherlands. This year, we mark 30 years since the CTBT opened for signature. The treaty stands today as a core element of the international nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regime. Its greatest achievement is clear, advancing a powerful global norm against nuclear testing. This norm has helped constrain nuclear proliferation and reduce nuclear threats. It's been reinforced by the treaty's verification regime, including an international monitoring system that has successfully detected declared nuclear explosive tests. Beyond its core mission, this system can help monitor nuclear accidents and provides data that supports responses to earthquakes, tsunamis, and volcanic activity. President, this year we celebrate the universalization of the CTBT across the Pacific region. We warmly welcome the recent signature and ratification by the Kingdom of Tonga. The universalization of the treaty is a significant milestone for a region that has experienced firsthand the humanitarian and environmental impacts of nuclear weapons testing. Following Tonga's ratification, a total of 188 states have now signed and 179 states have now ratified the CTBT. We applaud the Executive Secretary of the CTBTO Preparatory Commission, Dr. Robert Floyd, and his team for their tireless work to advance the universalization of the Treaty. We are determined to relegate nuclear testing to history by pursuing full ratification and implementation. But we know this endeavor faces serious challenges. We recall our condemnation of the six nuclear tests conducted by the DPRK since 2006. We strongly urge the DPRK not to conduct further testing. We call upon all States to refrain from any action that would defeat the object and purpose of the CTBT and to adopt or uphold national moratoria against all nuclear weapons tests, explosions and any other nuclear explosions. We underscore the importance of developing and implementing new concrete measures to restore confidence in these moratoria. Looking forward, we welcome the ongoing work to complete the CTBT's verification regime. We commend continued progress in strengthening the CTBTO's on-site inspection capabilities, which will provide the ultimate verification measure once the treaty enters into force. In this regard, we look forward to the integrated field exercise in Namibia in October and November and thank Namibia for hosting the exercise. Sustaining these verification capabilities requires financial support. At a time of significant financial pressure on the CTBTO, we urge all state signatories to pay their assessed contributions in full and on time. We remain committed to preserving the long-term effectiveness of the treaty's verification regime pending entry into force. President, the value of the CTBT is unquestionable, but we cannot take for granted the global norm against nuclear testing until it is legally binding. We urge all states that have not already done so to sign and ratify the treaty, particularly the nine Annex II states. The unprecedented decision by the Russian Federation to de-ratify the CTBT in 2023 represents a serious setback for efforts towards universalization. It further illustrates Russia's disregard for global arms control and non-proliferation efforts. We encourage state signatories to support continued efforts to strengthen the treaty and its verification regime and to achieve its entry into force as soon as possible. In support of this goal, we look forward once again to convening the ministerial meeting of the Friends of the CTBT on September 22 during the UN General Assembly high-level week. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Uruguay on behalf of the community of Latin American and Caribbean states.

Thank you, President. I'm particularly grateful for the convening of this meeting. Latin America and the Caribbean was the first region in which all states ratified the treaty. In this regard, we agree that the mere existence of nuclear weapons constitutes a threat to humanity and that the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons constitutes a crime against humanity and a violation of international law, including international humanitarian law and the United Nations Charter. We take this opportunity to warmly welcome Ambassador Juan Carlos Ojeda Villone, who assumed office as Secretary General of the Agency for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America and the Caribbean, OPANAL, on the 1st of January. We wish him every success in the exercise of his mandate and we reaffirm our full support to the work of OPANAL. No state must ever employ nuclear weapons under any circumstances. We call on all states to fully comply with their obligations under the disarmament and non-proliferation regime, including those contained in the NPT, the TPNW and the CTBT. We welcome the convening of the first review conference of the States Parties to the TPNW to be held in New York from the 30th of November to the 4th of December of this year, and we encourage States that have not yet ratified the Treaty to do so. We urge nuclear weapons States to fulfil all their obligations and commitments pursuant to the NPT, in particular those related to Article VI of the Treaty, as well as their unequivocal commitment to eliminate their nuclear arsenals. We note with concern that the 11th NPT Review Conference, which was held from the 27th of April to the 22nd of May of this year, was unable to agree a final document. This should strengthen, not diminish, our collective determination to preserve the treaty, as well as reinforce its implementation by all states parties, and advance concrete progress on nuclear disarmament, non-proliferation, and the peaceful use of nuclear energy. President, the effective prohibition of nuclear testing must remain an absolute priority. Our region will continue to advance nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation as a priority objective, consistent with the Treaty of Tlatelolco and the proclamation of Latin America and the Caribbean as a zone of peace that will contribute to the goal of a safer world free of nuclear weapons. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Qatar. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union on behalf of the EU and its member states.

Thank you, Mr. President. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the European Union and its member states. The candidate countries, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine, The Republic of Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Georgia, as well as Andorra and San Marino, aligned themselves with this statement. Nuclear test explosions represent a serious danger to international peace and security. The cessation of all nuclear weapon tests, explosions and all other nuclear explosions is an effective measure of nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation in all its aspects. The importance of these overarching objectives is today more acute than ever, as we face heightened global security risks. The breakdown of international law is evident in several crises facing the world. The EU condemns in the strongest possible terms Russia's actions, its nuclear rhetoric and its threats to use nuclear force in its illegal, unjustified and unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine. which are irresponsible, provocative, dangerous and escalatory. The CTBT is one of the key pillars of the international disarmament and non-proliferation architecture, contributing to global peace and security. The Treaty's strong legitimacy and vital importance for our collective security is enshrined in UN Security Council Resolution 2310 and the annual General Assembly resolutions relating to the CTBT. Since its opening for signature 30 years ago, the CTBT has served to limit nuclear testing in an unprecedented way, complementing the NPT and serving as a strong confidence and security building measure. The CTBT's entry into force remains a high priority for the European Union. This high level meeting provides another opportunity to call for the treaty's prompt entry into force and universalization. We warmly welcome the ratification of the CTBT by Tonga. Following DPRK's six nuclear tests, the CTBTO demonstrated its invaluable role in quickly providing reliable and independent data due to a truly global monitoring system for nuclear explosions. The EU urges the DPRK to comply with its obligations under relevant UN Security Council resolutions to refrain from testing nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles, and to abandon its existing programmes for nuclear weapons, ballistic missiles and other weapons of mass destruction in a complete, verifiable and irreversible manner, as required by several UN Security Council resolutions. We urge the DPRK to sign and ratify the CTBT without any precondition or further delay. The European Union reiterates its full confidence in the CTBT's verification regime, and looks forward to the completion of the international monitoring system. The completion and sustainment of IMS through adequate funding remains a priority, even in the context of a zero nominal growth budget, as it is crucial to maintain the network and ensure high data availability. The EU advocates for fully exploiting the potential benefits of civil and scientific applications of IMS data. The EU financially supports the CTBTO's verification regime and integrated capacity building activities in developing countries. Since 2006, the voluntary contributions of the European Union amounted to more than 36 million euro. President, as we mark this year the 30th anniversary of the opening for signature of the CTBT, We welcome the high-level events convened under the auspices of the Provisional Technical Secretariat in New York and Vienna, and the ministerial meeting organized by the Friends of the CTBT in the margins of the UN General Assembly in New York this September.

I thank the distinguished representative of the EU. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Philippines on behalf of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, followed by Kazakhstan and Costa Rica.

Thank you, Mr. President. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of ASEAN, the full version of which will be circulated. ASEAN reaffirms its unwavering commitment to strengthening multilateralism and international cooperation to contribute to global peace and security. We remain concerned over the growing risks of nuclear danger and conflict, the expansion and modernization of nuclear arsenals, and increasing salience of nuclear weapons in military and security doctrines. ASEAN underscores its commitment to the total elimination of nuclear weapons, which remain the only guarantee against their use, and the risk of catastrophic humanitarian consequences. ASEAN reaffirms its collective position against nuclear tests. As we mark the 30th anniversary of the CTBT, ASEAN stresses the importance of universal ratification to the treaty without delay. All ASEAN member states have ratified the CTBT, and we urge the remaining Annex II states to sign and ratify it as soon as possible to realize its entry into force. pending its entry into force, ASEAN also urges all nuclear weapons states to maintain at minimum a moratorium on nuclear explosive testing. ASEAN remains mindful of the situation in all regions that underwent nuclear test explosions, and we encourage the international community to assist these regions. ASEAN reaffirms the NPT as the cornerstone of global nuclear disarmament, non-proliferation, and peaceful use of nuclear energy. We regret that the 11th NPT Review Conference was unable to adopt a consensus outcome document. We commend Vietnam for its leadership as President of the Conference. We express concern over the declining commitment and cooperation in global non-proliferation, arms control and disarmament mechanisms, and call on countries, especially nuclear weapon states, to maintain and fully implement their commitments under these mechanisms, including the NPT. who continue to call on the nuclear weapon states to fulfill their obligations under Article VI and agreed commitments of the NPT review conferences. It is crucial for the nuclear weapon states to adhere to legally binding negative security assurances and adopt the no first use policy regarding nuclear weapons, as well as to pursue risk reduction strategies to prevent unintentional or accidental use of such weapons. Additionally, the nuclear weapon states must make an unequivocal commitment not to use or threaten to use nuclear weapons against non-nuclear weapon states. ASEAN maintains that the TPNW is an historic agreement which contributes towards global nuclear disarmament and complements the NPT, CTBT and other existing nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation instruments. We underscore the immense contribution of nuclear weapons-free zones to nuclear disarmament, non-proliferation, and international peace and security. We reaffirm our commitment to preserving Southeast Asia as a nuclear weapons-free zone and to the full and effective implementation of the TPNWS Treaty, including through its Plan of Action. We remain committed to engaging all nuclear weapons states, including those with reservations, and to resolving outstanding issues in accordance with objectives and principles of the treaty. ASEAN notes ongoing efforts to explore the possibility of individual nuclear weapons states signing and ratifying the protocol without reservations and welcomes those ready to do so. ASEAN remains gravely concerned over the recent surge in the DPRK's intercontinental ballistic missile testing and ballistic missile launches and the increased tension in the Korean peninsula. We call on the DPRK to fully comply with all relevant UN Security Council resolutions and call for peaceful dialogue towards lasting peace and stability in a denuclearized Korean Peninsula. Diplomatic efforts should remain a priority and ASEAN reiterates its readiness to play a constructive role through ASEAN-led platforms, including the ASEAN Regional Forum. In conclusion, Mr. President, the United Nations remains an indispensable platform for fostering trust and confidence and upholding peace and security. Let us work together to ensure that the horrors of nuclear testing remain a relic of the past and realize the goal of a world without nuclear weapons for all. Thank you, Mr. President.

I thank the distinguished representative of the Philippines, I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Kazakhstan on behalf of the Central Asian states, followed by Costa Rica and Timor-Leste.

Mr. President, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the states parties to the treaty on a nuclear weapon free zone in Central Asia, namely the Kyrgyz Republic, the Republic of Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, the Republic of Uzbekistan, and my own country, the Republic of Kazakhstan, that serves as chair of the treaty. We welcome the high-level plenary meeting to commemorate and promote the International Day Against Nuclear Tests. This year marks the 20th anniversary of the signing of the treaty in Semipalatinsk on September 8, 2006. The choice of Semipalatinsk reflected the history of Central Asia as a region where nuclear weapons had been tested and stationed. The treaty gave legal effect to the common decision of the five Central Asian states to exclude nuclear weapons from the region through cooperation and verifiable commitments. We also urge all interested parties to consider providing appropriate assistance to the Central Asian states for radiological assessment and remediation of the former nuclear test sites and uranium tailing storage sites. The security of the zone is reinforced by the protocol to the treaty. We welcome its signature by all five nuclear weapons states and its ratification by China, France, the Russian Federation, and the United Kingdom. We express hope for the earliest ratification by the United States, thereby completing the framework of legally binding security assurances for the zone. The 20th anniversary of the Semipalatinsk Treaty coincides with the 30th anniversary of the opening for the signature of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. All five Central Asian states have ratified the CTBT and remain firmly committed to its universalization and entry into force. We urge all states that have not yet done so, particularly remaining Annex II states, to sign and ratify the CTBT without delay. Pending its entry into force, all states should maintain existing moratoria on nuclear weapon tests and any other nuclear explosions, and refrain from actions contrary to the objective and purposes of the treaty. Moratoria remain important but cannot replace a permanent, legally binding and effectively verifiable prohibition. The Central Asian states remain committed to strengthening cooperation with other nuclear-weapon-free zones. On this 20th anniversary, the five Central Asian states reaffirm their commitment to the full implementation of the Simi Polatins Treaty and strengthening of the international norm against nuclear testing and the achievement of a world free of nuclear weapons. Mr. President, now I would like to make a few remarks in my national capacity. This year marks 35 years since the closure of the Semipalatinsk test site. As you heard from the victim of nuclear testing, Karibek Kuyukov, between 1949 and 1989, 456 nuclear tests were conducted there. Over a million people were affected and extensive territories were exposed to radioactive contamination. The consequences still remain present in affected communities and land and will stay like this for a foreseeable future. In recognition of the lasting consequences of nuclear tests, Kazakhstan initiated General Assembly Resolution 64/35, which unanimously proclaimed 29th of August as the International Day Against Nuclear Tests. Kazakhstan also welcomes the international meeting on victim assistance and environmental remediation to be convened tomorrow pursuant to General Assembly Resolution 80/56. It should strengthen practical cooperation among affected states, international organizations, scientific institutions, affected communities, and civil society. Kazakhstan will continue cooperating with Dr. Robert Floyd and other partners to secure the entry into force of the CTBT, strengthen assistance to affected communities, and advance the complete elimination of nuclear weapons. I thank you.

Mr. President, Morocco commends you for convening this meeting and thanks the briefers we heard today. 30 years after the CTBT opened for signature, the international security environment has become more demanding. Instruments of strategic restraint patiently built over decades are under strain. The 11th NPT Review Conference concluded in May without a consensus outcome, and the question of nuclear testing has returned to public debate after many years of silence. Morocco does not approach this moment in a spirit of reproach. The restraint that has prevailed in this field over a long period is a collective achievement, patiently built and preserved. My country values it and is convinced that its consolidation serves the security of every Member State. In that spirit, Morocco wishes to underline three priorities. First, universality and entry into force. With full respect for the sovereign prerogative of each Member State, Morocco renews its appeal to all Member States that have not yet joined the treaty to consider doing so. Entry into force would give the existing moratoria the permanence that only a treaty can provide. Second, the verification regime, whose value extends well beyond the treaty itself. With 307 of its 337 facilities certified, the international monitoring system has become one of the most remarkable scientific infrastructures ever placed at the service of the international community. Its data supports tsunami warning, earthquake response, environmental monitoring and research benefits that reach every region and every member state regardless of its position on the treaty. Morocco is associated with this collective endeavor through the auxiliary system seismic station of Midelt, which forms part of this network and considers the completion and the durability of the system to be in the interest of all. Third, the preservation of the collective capacities built around this regime. The training of experts, the readiness of inspection procedures, the transmission of scientific knowledge and the engagement of younger generations are important investments. Morocco supports their continuity, remains attached to the spirit of cooperation and dialogue that has always allowed progress in this field. Few of these organizations' undertakings carry as much hope as the ambition of a world free of nuclear tests. That ambition is not remote. It already exists in a treaty signed by the overwhelming majority of nations, in a verification system that functions every day, and in a body of scientific and human expertise that continues to grow. What remains is to give it its final form. Morocco hopes that this assembly will one day be able to state, with the full authority of a treaty in force, that this chapter of history is definitely closed. Morocco will continue to accompany every effort directed to that end. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Morocco. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of China.

President, The complete prohibition and thorough destruction of nuclear weapons, the elimination of the threat of nuclear war, and the ultimate establishment of a world free of nuclear weapons are in the common interest of humanity. The nuclear disarmament process faces serious setbacks while the risk of a nuclear arms race and a nuclear conflict continue to rise. This year marks the 30th anniversary of the opening for signature of the CTBT. The ban on nuclear testing has now become a universal consensus within the international community. All countries should resolutely uphold the treaty's vital role in curbing the nuclear arms race and reducing the risk of a nuclear war, and work together to build a world of lasting peace and universal security. Nuclear weapons states should strictly abide by their commitment to suspend nuclear testing, reduce the status and role of nuclear weapons in their national security strategies, and explicitly commit to, among other things, a no-first-use policy. As one of the first countries to sign the CTBT, China has consistently and firmly supported the treaty's purposes and objectives, strictly adhered to its commitment to suspension of nuclear testing, worked to uphold the international consensus on nuclear testing ban, and supported relevant international efforts, thereby making significant contributions to maintaining the treaty's universality and authority. China has long maintained a high degree of stability, continuity and predictability in its nuclear policy. We adhere to a policy of no first use of nuclear weapons and have unconditionally committed not to use or threaten to use nuclear weapons against non-nuclear weapon states or nuclear weapon free zones. China's nuclear forces constitute an indispensable element in deterring nuclear war and maintaining world peace, security and global strategic stability. China is willing to continue to work with all parties to promote the early entry into force of the CTBT, uphold the authority of the NPT, safeguard the international nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regime. regime and make unremitting efforts to achieve the noble goal of the complete prohibition and total elimination of nuclear weapons. I thank the distinguished representative of China. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia, followed by Thailand and Sweden.

Indonesia aligns itself with the statement delivered by the Philippines on behalf of ASEAN and wishes to add the following points on our national capacity. First, we must preserve and strengthen the global norm against nuclear testing. Thanks to CTBT, the landscape of nuclear testing today is very different from 30 years ago. Since its adoption in 1996, a strong global norm against nuclear testing has taken hold. Indonesia is proud to have contributed to this progress by ratifying the treaty in 2012 as an annex to state. It was a clear declaration of our commitment to a world free of nuclear weapons. Second, we must respond to new challenges, powerful computers, AI, advanced simulations, and non-explosive experiments allow nuclear-armed states to assess and maintain their nuclear arsenals without conducting nuclear explosions. I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Thailand, followed by Sweden and Vietnam.

Thank you, Mr. President. Thailand aligns itself with the statement delivered by the Philippines on behalf of ASEAN and wishes to add the following in its national capacity. Given today's heightened geopolitical tensions, the risk of the resumption of nuclear testing poses a grave threat to international peace and security. Any return to nuclear testing would severely erode the global non-proliferation architecture and reverse decades of hard-won progress. To address these challenges, Thailand highlights three key priorities. First, we must achieve the universalization of the CTBT. Thailand urges all remaining Annex II states and nuclear weapons states to exercise utmost restraint uphold their testing moratoria, and ratify the treaty without delay. We welcome Tonga's recent ratification, completing universalization in the Pacific, and hope that this momentum inspires others to follow suit. Second, we must reinforce the disarmament framework. Global nuclear disarmament and regional security are intrinsically linked. Thailand firmly believes that the CTBT, NPT, TPNW, and other regional nuclear weapon-free zone treaties, including the Shan Fez Treaty, are mutually reinforcing instruments to achieving our shared objective of a world free of nuclear weapons. Third, we must demonstrate concrete technical leadership. Thailand has consistently translated our commitment into action. We operate two international monitoring system stations and look forward to hosting Southeast Asia's first noble gas detection facility once the upgrade is completed. Furthermore, the visit of Dr. Robert Floyd to Thailand last July deepened our cooperation and reaffirmed our joint effort to build robust technical capacity across the region. Mr. President, as we commemorate the International Day Against Nuclear Tests and the 30th anniversary of the CTBT, the treaty remains as critically relevant as ever. It is indeed time to renew our collective commitment to bring the CTBT into force and end nuclear testing once and for all. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Thailand and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Sweden.

Thank you, Mr. President. Excellencies, colleagues, Sweden fully aligns itself with the EU statement. and I have the honor to present the following remarks in my national capacity. Given the present global security situation and the pressure on the disarmament and non-proliferation architecture, strengthening existing disarmament and non-proliferation tools is essential. The Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty is one such instrument. Sweden currently serves as co-president of the Article 14 process of the CTBT. This reflects our firm commitment to the treaty and its crucial role in the global disarmament and non-proliferation regime. This year marks the CTBT's 30th anniversary with key achievements. First, Near universal support, 188 signatories and 179 ratifications, including the most recent accession of Tonga in July, which completes adherence to the CTBT across the Pacific region. The international monitoring system and data center has detected all DPRK tests and has provided rapid information. President, the milestones we are commemorating this year remind us that progress in disarmament and non-proliferation requires sustained political will and a renewed commitment to multilateralism. Our common objective of a safe

The delegation of Ukraine aligns itself with the EU statement. We would like to add some additional remarks in our national capacity. Mr. President, Austria aligns itself with the statements presented by the EU and WIIOG. This International Day Against Nuclear Tests is no ordinary one. At a time of heightened global tension and rising nuclear threats, we must take the strongest stand against the threat of nuclear weapons and all nuclear testing. Today, the danger of nuclear conflict is higher than at any time since the Cold War. This goes beyond testing. As long as nuclear weapons exist, they remain an existential threat to every nation and every person. We reject any and all nuclear threats, explicit or implicit. The use or threat of use of nuclear weapons is a grave breach of international law and the UN Charter. The majority of states want a world free from nuclear risk. The TPNW, which Austria co-initiated and consistently champions, puts the humanitarian consequences and unacceptable risks of nuclear weapons at the forefront. Awareness of these catastrophic consequences must underpin all disarmament efforts. The TPNW also prohibits nuclear tests, thus strengthening the global norm against testing. We look forward to its first review conference this December, a crucial opportunity to consolidate the treaty's trajectory and advance its universalization. Austria is honored to host the CTBTO in Vienna and to support its critical work under the able leadership of Executive Secretary Robert Floyd. Our commitment is grounded in the belief in the intersection of diplomacy and science that made the CTBT possible. The record of the past century speaks for itself. It is the result of decades of effort by states, scientists, and the CTBTO. But this success is fragile. Any test at any yield would undermine the norm, erode trust, and threaten decades of progress. Mr. President, In the face of geopolitical strains, a renewed arms race and the weakening of the nuclear taboo, the CTBT is not just a treaty. It's a shield. Strengthening it is not just a choice. It's a moral and strategic imperative. This anniversary is an opportunity to recommit to the CTBT as our technical and normative shield against nuclear testing, to its entry into force with its on-site inspections and compliance mechanisms. We need political will and sustainable financial support, and also consider ways to even further improve the sensitivity of the international monitoring system. Austria remains fully committed to this mission, and I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Cambodia and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of South Africa.

President, South Africa associates with the statement delivered on behalf of the African Group. A growing body of scientific evidence and the testimonies of affected communities, as we've heard this morning, continue to demonstrate the devastating harm and long-term risks associated with the testing and use of nuclear weapons. It is therefore deeply regrettable that 30 years after the CTBT was opened for signature, it has yet to enter into force. This remains the case despite the catastrophic humanitarian and environmental consequences of the nuclear detonations in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, as well as the experiences of communities affected by more than 2,000 nuclear tests conducted worldwide. The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons was adopted as a response and to address based on scientific evidence the catastrophic humanitarian consequences of a nuclear weapon detonation. By prohibiting the development, testing, production, possession and transfer of nuclear weapons and other nuclear explosive devices, the TPNW complements both the CTBT and the Treaty on Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. President, the world cannot afford a nuclear detonation, whether by accident or intention due to the catastrophic humanitarian and environmental consequences, as well as the threat to international peace and security. South Africa therefore reaffirms the imperative of prohibiting all nuclear tests, explosions, ending the development and qualitative and quantitative improvement of nuclear weapons and completely eliminating nuclear weapons. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of South Africa. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Fiji.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Fiji speaks today not only as an advocate against nuclear testing, but as a state that has lived its consequences. We will not rehearse that history here. We will speak instead about what this assembly must do now. Thirty years ago, Fiji became the first state in the world to ratify the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. We did not wait, not because we are powerful, but because we knew what was at stake. This year, the Pacific completed what Fiji began, and we congratulate the Kingdom of Tonga, whose ratification in July deliver the universal adherence across our Pacific region. But let us be honest about this moment. This Thursday marks nine years to the day since the last nuclear explosion anywhere on earth. The longest silence since 1945. And yet, test sites are maintained, tunnels are kept in readiness, and the language of resumption has returned. Fiji says plainly, No state's conduct justifies another state's test. There is only fallout, and it does not distinguish between the powerful and the small. Fiji therefore calls on all states, maintain the moratorium without conditions, and without waiting to see who moves first. Ratify the treaty. Nine of the 44 Annex II states remain outstanding. And 30 years is long enough. Sustain the international monitoring system, which keeps watch on behalf of everyone, including those who have not yet joined it, and meet the obligations owed for testing already done, remediation, health care, and recognition for those who never consented to it. Fiji was the first to ratify. We will not be the last to insist. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Fiji. We have had the last speaker in the commemorative meeting for this morning. We shall hear the remaining speakers tomorrow, 1st of September in this hall after the program announced in the journal. The exercise of the right of reply has been requested. As announced in the president's letters dated 6th January and 20th May, 2026, I propose that the time limits for statements in the exercise of the right of reply under this item be limited to five minutes for the first intervention and to three minutes for the second intervention. Is there any objection to this proposal? I hear none. It is so decided. Accordingly, pursuant to Rule 72 of the Rules of Procedure of the Assembly, when a representative exceeds her or his allotted time, the President shall call the speaker to order without delay, which will be done by means of automatic microphone cutoff. To assist delegations in managing their time, a countdown clock will be displayed on the screens. Members are also reminded that statements in the exercise of the right of reply should be made by delegations from their seats. I now give the floor to -- I call on the representative of the Russian Federation.

President, We regret that some member states are using the GA, this platform, to make anti-Russian insinuations divorced from reality. We renounce, denounce any allegations leveled at Russia, including comments made by the EU delegation related to the situation, the situation surrounding the CTBT. We've stated our position on many occasions the reason why we revoked our ratification of the CTBT, we'll have to do it again. Given the deterioration in the international security space surrounding the CTBT, the situation is now very difficult. There's no likelihood of the treaty entering into force, but it's not Russia's fault as colleagues are trying to suggest. Various US administrations have used trumped up justifications to reject ratification of the treaty, Washington has not taken any steps to move closer to ratification. Without a doubt, the US is not interested in the ratification of this treaty. And in 2025, the president himself, the president of the US, said that there's a need to resume nuclear tests alongside other states. After that statement, they increased funding to relevant chapters of the US budget. For that reason, we'd like to warn about the fact that if the US rejected the moratorium on tests, well, that could have a domino effect under these circumstances. And also in light of the overall political context, Russia believed the imbalance between Russia and the US as regards CTBT obligations was no longer tenable, we fixed the situation by revoking our ratification. I am referring to us revoking the ratification, I want to emphasize that. We have signed the CTBT, we're a signatory thereto with all of the rights and obligations stemming therefrom. For example, we are upholding the moratorium on nuclear tests introduced back when we still had the USSR in 1990. In December of 2023, we completed the building of the Russian segment of the international monitoring system. It comprises, is comprised of 32 facilities. We continue to work with the technical secretariat of the CTBTO to ensure that the facilities I mentioned earlier continue working uninterrupted. Thank you for your kind attention.
I now call on the representative of Israel for a second intervention. Israel for their fast intervention.

Mr. President, we have heard some remarks regarding nuclear disarmament and the Middle East that are detached from the current reality in the region. We call those who made the remarks to update their policy statements and devote more time and efforts to pursuing a Middle East where all countries recognize each other's right to exist. I thank you, Mr. President.
The Assembly has thus concluded this stage of its consideration of agenda item 99. The meeting is adjourned.
